p1-v1.alt: Surveyor 3 on a stand in a laboratory, next to a console with screens and buttons.

textos.texto: 1967. Before sending astronauts, NASA needed to know what the Moon's ground was like.
Will the lunar ground be hard or soft?

p1-v2.alt: A rocket lifts off next to an orange launch tower, surrounded by clouds of smoke.

textos.texto: April 17, 1967. Surveyor 3 lifts off from Florida aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket.

p1-v3.alt: Surveyor 3 travels through space along a dotted line from Earth to the Moon.

textos.texto: Its mission: land gently, take photos and study the lunar ground.
The Moon is getting closer and closer!

p1-v4.alt: Surveyor 3 descends over the gray lunar ground with its engine firing, kicking up dust.

textos.texto: Three days later, it was descending toward the Ocean of Storms…
Firing my brakes!

p2-v1.alt: Three images of Surveyor 3 joined by curved arrows: the spacecraft bounces twice on the lunar ground.

textos.texto: April 20, 1967. When it touched down, its engines kept firing: it bounced twice before coming to a stop!
Boing! Boing!

p2-v2.alt: Surveyor 3, now still on the Moon, sends radio waves to a smiling Earth in the sky.

textos.texto: At last, at rest! From Earth, the team checked that everything was working.
Surveyor 3 here: all good!

p2-v3.alt: A close-up of Surveyor 3 next to a photo of the lunar landscape with mountains and craters.

textos.texto: Its camera began sending photos of the lunar landscape.
Click, click!

p2-v4.alt: Surveyor 3's arm with a scoop digs a trench in the lunar ground.

textos.texto: Its mechanical scoop dug trenches to test how firm the ground was. Firm enough for spacecraft with astronauts to land!
The ground holds up!

p3-v1.alt: Surveyor 3 sends radio waves and small photos flying toward Earth.

textos.texto: Surveyor 3 sent 6,315 photos to Earth. They helped us learn much more about the lunar ground.

p3-v2.alt: A sleepy Surveyor 3 in the darkness of the lunar night; Earth appears in the sky as a thin crescent.

textos.texto: May 4, 1967: its last communication. The lunar night had begun, and it lasts about two weeks. Without sunlight, it shut down.
Good night, Earth…

p3-v3.alt: Two astronauts next to Surveyor 3: one kneeling and one waving; the lunar module stands in the background.

textos.texto: November 1969. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean, of Apollo 12, landed nearby and went to visit it.
Hello, Surveyor! We finally found you!

p3-v4.alt: An astronaut carries Surveyor 3's camera; the spacecraft remains on the Moon and Earth waves.

textos.texto: They took its camera and other parts back to Earth to study them. Surveyor 3 is still on the Moon: its data helped prepare for astronauts to land.
This camera is going home!

cierre.datoReal: Apollo 12 landed about 180 meters from Surveyor 3: a precision landing! The astronauts visited it about two and a half years after it arrived.
cierre.preguntaAula: Why do you think NASA sent robots to the Moon before people?
